lessons.title: The Latency Budget — Where the Time Actually Goes

children.text: Ask an HFT engineer where their microseconds go and you rarely get a single number. You get a list. Latency is not one measurement, it is a budget spent across five or six different stops between a price tick leaving the exchange and a firm's order landing back on it. Understanding that budget matters more than knowing any single headline latency figure.

markDefs.definition: A technique where an application reads and writes network packets directly from the network card's memory, skipping the operating system's normal network stack to cut processing time.

children.text: Once a firm has paid for colocation, physical distance stops being the main problem. What is left is a chain of software and hardware stops inside the firm's own server, and each one eats into the tick-to-trade budget. One of the biggest levers here is
: letting the trading application talk to the network card directly instead of routing every packet through the operating system's standard network stack.

body.caption: Illustrative latency budget for a colocated strategy, before optimization

cells: Signal travels the physical distance between racks and to the exchange gateway
The network card and operating system move the packet into and out of application memory
The trading application decides whether and how to respond
The firm's own pre-trade risk controls validate the order before it leaves the firm's network
The exchange's gateway and matching engine receive, validate, and acknowledge the order

body.text: Colocation buys proximity. It does not automatically buy speed. Two firms sitting in racks a few metres apart inside the same exchange data centre can have very different tick-to-trade numbers, because the difference now lives entirely in how each one has engineered its own software and hardware stack.

body.title: A Latency Audit Checklist
steps: Timestamp every hop with a hardware clock, not just application-level software time.
Move the trading application off the kernel's standard network stack wherever the risk framework allows it.
Pin latency-critical threads to isolated CPU cores so the operating system scheduler cannot interrupt them.
Profile the strategy logic path end to end, not just its average case.
Measure order gateway and pre-trade risk check time separately from the exchange's own matching engine time.

body.label: Network Propagation Inside a Colo Facility
body.context: Time for a signal to travel a few hundred metres of fibre within the exchange's own data centre. Effectively fixed once a firm is colocated, which is why the fight moves to hardware and software.

body.text: Once you are colocated, the exchange stops being the bottleneck. Your own server becomes one.

points: Tick-to-trade latency is not one number, it is a budget spent across network propagation, NIC and kernel processing, strategy logic, order gateway checks, and exchange-side processing.
Colocation mainly buys down network propagation delay to a near-fixed, very small number. It does not by itself buy down the rest of the budget.
Kernel bypass, hardware timestamping, and core pinning are software and hardware techniques used to shrink the largest remaining chunks of the budget.
The next two chapters cover the two big levers for shrinking this budget: colocation itself (Chapter 2) and the network and hardware choices firms make once they are inside it (Chapter 3).
